items.title: Pro-Life Group Reportedly Kicked Out of Coffee Shop, Compared to KKK
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an Idaho coffee shop after the owner learned she was holding a meeting there.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, shared a video of what purportedly took place at Wydaho Roasters last month — and that video went viral.

Hawkins told CBN News that coffee shop owner Jim Sheehan made his displeasure known after she, her son, and others met to discuss pro-life issues inside Wydaho Roasters. Her son’s goal has been to rally people against Proposition 1, an abortion measure that will be on the ballot in November.

“We’re recruiting door knockers, and we’ve had students going door to door, educating people in Idaho about this extreme abortion ballot referendum, which sadly many people don’t know about,” Hawkins said, noting her son rallied people online to come meet to form a pro-life group to address the issue.

The coffee shop was the intended gathering place for the group’s first meeting, but that didn’t go very well.

“We had purchased our drinks and our food,” she said. “Some other leaders, community members, came to kind of join the group that I knew from church.”

According to Hawkins, Sheehan came out of his office and told the group they couldn’t meet at the shop and needed to leave. Hawkins took out her camera and started filming the interaction, hoping she could simply convince the owner to let them stay for the first meeting and then pledge not to return.

“I was trying to negotiate with him, just like, let us finish this meeting; we won’t come back,” she said. “And then he just kept going and then compared us to the KKK and said, we were like the KKK, that pro-lifers were like the KKK, which was just beyond the pale. And that’s actually why I decided to release the video.”

Hawkins made it clear that she believes, as an owner, Sheehan has the right to refuse service and was within his rights to ask the group to leave. That said, she also believes in her right to expose his purported comparison between the pro-life activists and the KKK.

The result of the entire escapade was intense media coverage and viral video discussion. Ultimately, both Hawkins and Sheehan reportedly started getting death threats.

“He was well within his rights to kick us out,” Hawkins said. “I was within my rights to expose his insanity, believing that community members were like the KKK, but neither of us deserves to die or receive death threats.”

Sheehan told Fox News that he pushes back on claims the group was kicked out. He said he had asked via Facebook the day before that the group not meet in his coffee shop.

“Sunday she announced on a local community page they were holding this meeting at our business, naming it — I responded to the post politely asking them not to use our business as the agenda of the organization does not align with us,” he told the outlet. “They showed up anyway.”

items.title: Christian Grandma Refuses to Back Down After Government Demands She Stop Feeding Community
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: What started as a woman feeling called to cook breakfast for a handful of friends has turned into a dispute […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

What started as a woman feeling called to cook breakfast for a handful of friends has turned into a dispute over food, faith, and government regulations.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kathy Kite, a resident of Harrisburg, Missouri, began welcoming locals into her home for breakfast back in May after the community’s convenience store stopped serving breakfast following COVID.

Kite works at H-Town, the local convenience store and gas station, and said residents had repeatedly expressed interest in finding a new place to have breakfast. She lives nearby, so she decided to offer an alternative by cooking for her friends and offering up the food for free.

“I told the old guys that come in there in the mornings that like to play cards, and drink coffee, and eat breakfast, and say they didn’t have any more — I’m like, ‘You guys can come to my house and I’ll do it,’” Kite told CBN News.

So, she started offering breakfast out of her kitchen and people came.

“It all started with just some like sausage, egg, and cheese biscuits,” Kite said.

At first, it was just a few people. But others soon began to come after her loving act was advertised on social media, with 20-25 people regularly coming to her home in the morning; some parents even brought their kids to her house for food before school. Kite gets up at 3:30 a.m. to prepare for the day.

“And it just kind of exploded from there,” Kite said. “So then people were like, ‘Breakfast? We have breakfast in town?’”

Kite doesn’t charge for the meals. There is a place for people to leave money if they choose, but she said those contributions go back into buying ingredients and food.

“It’s not a moneymaker by any means,” she said.

For Kite, feeding people is also deeply connected to her Christian faith.

“For whatever reason, God has put it in my heart that I need to take care of people,” she said. “I like to feed people.”

Kite continued, “In my mind feeding people is loving people.”

But Kite’s breakfast gatherings eventually caught the attention of government officials, with Columbia city officials from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department reportedly sending a letter telling her she needed a commercial kitchen license to continue operating.

Kite disputes that she is operating a business, though, and said the government’s demands have broken her heart.

“I’m not running a business,” she said. “This is just friends coming over for breakfast. It’s no different than a backyard barbecue or a church gathering.”

Kite said the warning dramatically affected attendance, as some residents became concerned that continuing to visit could cause additional trouble for her. As a result, many stopped coming.

“I went from having probably 20 to 25 to maybe 5 to 8 people,” she said.

Still, Kite isn’t planning to stop, despite admitting she was scared to incur fines or worse. Rather than back down, she sought legal help and has no plans to stop.

“God laid this on me and I just feel like if God brought me to it, God’s going to bring me through it,” Kite said. “I believe in what I’m doing. I don’t believe I’m doing anything wrong.”

The Goldwater Institute is helping Kite and has sent a letter to the Boone County health department seeking answers about why they are demanding a commercial kitchen. Officials with the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News that Kite has a tip jar, open sign, and is advertising food on social media, indicating elements “associated with a food establishment.”

“No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued. We also did not threaten jail time,” the statement read. “We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses.”

The text continued, “There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community.”

items.title: Skilla Baby’s Prayer Alarm Went Off on ‘The Breakfast Club,’ So the Whole Studio Stopped and Prayed With Him
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Skilla Baby was in the middle of an interview on “The Breakfast Club” Tuesday morning when his phone went off. It wasn’t a call. “It’s time for the prayer, too,” he said. “My prayer time.” Charlamagne tha God offered to stop. “You want to stop an
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Skilla Baby was in the middle of an interview on “The Breakfast Club” Tuesday morning when his phone went off. It wasn’t a call.

“It’s time for the prayer, too,” he said. “My prayer time.”

Charlamagne tha God offered to stop.

“You want to stop and pray? We can.”

“Yeah, come on. You’re gonna do it. Let’s do it. You’re gonna pray, or you want us to pray?”

“I want y’all to do it,” Skilla Baby said.

So the show stopped. The hosts got out of their chairs, gathered in a circle in the middle of the studio and held hands, and co-host Loren LoRosa prayed out loud.

“Dear Lord, Heavenly Father, thank you for bringing us together today. I thank you for Skilla Baby and his journey and his voice. I pray that you cover him. You continue to lead him down a path of leadership, but also down a path of vulnerability as he places his life story out for other people to see, to know, to understand, but also to follow in the right way.”

“I also pray that you comfort him in moments where we don’t even understand what comfort is, where he may not understand what comfort is, but that you sit right there next to him. You speak to him. You hold him in the ways that he is needed.”

“I pray no spirit of confusion, no spirit of fear, and I just pray that you continue to show favor in his life. I know that he is here for a reason. I know that he is still here with us for a reason.”

In May of last year, Skilla Baby’s SUV was hit with more than 25 rounds in a drive-by in Redford Township, just outside Detroit. He was struck three times and needed multiple surgeries.

He has said since that the shooting was not the hard part. Getting shot was “easy,” he told Complex, compared to the mental health battles he has had most of his life. Gospel singer Erica Campbell and her church, he has said, walked him through a dark stretch afterward.

The album he came on the show to promote is called The Price of Fame.

“Beautiful prayer, Loren,” Charlamagne said when it was over. “Skilla Baby, keep growing, my brother.”

items.title: Rethinking the Binding Nature of Religion
items.author: Dr. Richard Clements
items.summary:
Dr. Richard Clements

Rather than cramping our freedom, the Christian moral code expands and elevates human freedom, enabling us to share in the infinite freedom of God, the freedom of self-giving love.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard Clements

The human race has had somewhat of a love/hate relationship with religion. Some people find their deepest sense of identity, meaning, and purpose in religious belief, while others reject religious belief as mere superstition, infantile projection, wish-fulfillment, etc. It turns out that at least some of the reasons for these polarized reactions to religion are revealed by the etymology of the word “religion” itself.

Several different derivations for the word “religion” have been proposed over the centuries. Cicero suggested that the word was derived from the Latin word relegere, meaning “to treat or consider carefully”: “Those who carefully took in hand all things pertaining to the gods were called religiosi, from relegere.”

But the more likely derivation is from the Latin word religare (with “ligare” meaning “to bind” or “to connect” and “re-” meaning “again” or “back”). This was the derivation suggested by Lactantius, who wrote, “We are tied to God and bound to Him [religati] by the bond of piety.”

St. Augustine, after first proposing and then rejecting an alternative derivation, eventually came to agree with Lactantius’s claim, noting, “Religion binds us [religat] to the one Almighty God,” and Lactantius’s derivation is the one that is listed in many contemporary dictionaries.

Thus, the term “religion” most likely derives from a word that meant to “connect again” or to “bind again.” The idea of being connected appeals to many of us but being bound? Not so much. Many of us want to be connected to God, to a transcendent source of goodness, blessing, power, and eternal life. But for some people, the concept of being bound to God carries with it the negative connotations of being tied down, having limits placed upon their freedom, and having obligations imposed on them, and they tend to bristle at such perceived restrictions.

In fact, it is precisely this idea of “binding,” interpreted in the sense of restricting or limiting human freedom and blocking the fulfillment of our human potential, that has led some thinkers to reject religion out of hand.

Ludwig Feuerbach thought that the Christian God was a mere illusion onto which human beings projected both their deepest needs (e.g., love, protection, consolation) and their highest ideal attributes (including, once again, love, as well as wisdom, justice, and knowledge). Feuerbach claimed that religious belief functions as an obstacle to what he called our “species being,” by which he meant that religion blocks the fulfillment of human potential.

In Feuerbach’s estimation, religion makes human beings dependent on God rather than themselves, diminishes their confidence in their own abilities, and distracts them from focusing on this earthly life and on efforts to improve earthly society. He believed that man had the power to bring about his own salvation. Feuerbach’s claims exerted significant influence on several subsequent thinkers’ attitudes toward religion, including Karl Marx, Friedrich Nietzsche, Sigmund Freud, and Jean-Paul Sartre, all of whom rejected religion and caused many other people to reject religion as well. 

Roger Scruton, the British philosopher and cultural commentator, disagreed with Feuerbach and these other thinkers in regard to their rejection of religion. He argued that rather than being an obstacle to our “species being,” religion stems from our species being. Human beings, according to Scruton, have an innate need for religion: an innate need for connection to each other, to our forebears and to our progeny, and to the transcendent, and religion helps to facilitate those connections and those relationships.

But Scruton also valued the “binding” aspect of religion in the sense that religions typically impose a moral code upon their adherents, a code that often encourages such qualities as the assumption of personal responsibility for one’s actions, accountability to other people and to God for those actions, and a spirit of self-sacrifice, all of which are conducive to the formation and flourishing of human communities and of individual human beings.

Scruton was on the right track with his focus on both of these aspects of religion: the personal and societal benefits of the moral codes propounded by various religions, and also the experience of connection and relationship that is provided by religion. But we find a much deeper and more explicitly Christian explanation of and justification for these aspects of religion in the thought of Pope Benedict XVI.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Pope Benedict XVI certainly agreed with Scruton regarding the fundamental importance of the moral code provided by religion; on numerous occasions, he spoke out strongly against the moral relativism that is rampant in contemporary society and the damage that this relativism has done, both to individual people and to society. Individuals, and society as a whole, cannot survive and thrive in the long run without a sound moral code to guide their actions.

But Pope Benedict also emphasized that the purpose of the Christian moral code is not merely to conduce the flourishing of individual persons and of society; that code is meant to conform each of us to the image of Jesus Christ, the God-man (Rom. 8:28—30; 1 Cor. 15:49). The Christian moral code is meant to align our hearts, our minds, our actions, and our very being with the essence of God, who is goodness itself, so that we might participate as fully as possible in the divine life.

Rather than cramping our freedom, as is claimed by some opponents of Christianity, the Christian moral code expands and elevates human freedom, enabling us to share in the infinite freedom of God, which is the freedom of self-giving love. It is actually in being “bound” to God that we find our deepest freedom.

The Christian moral code is meant to teach us to love as God loves, so that we might be connected as closely as possible to God and to our fellow human beings. This leads us to the other and more profound meaning of the term “religion”: connection and relationship. As Pope Benedict so eloquently described, life is all about relationships. Relationship is a fundamental aspect of life, a fundamental aspect of existence itself, because relationship is a fundamental aspect of God, as is revealed in the Trinitarian nature of the Christian God. Relationship is not just an aspect or a characteristic of God; relationship is of the essence of God. Relationship is central to who and what God is. And since we human beings are made imago Dei, in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26—27), relationship is fundamental to who we are and who we are meant to be. We are hard-wired for relationship: relationship with our fellow human beings and relationship with God. That is one of the reasons why religion has been such a pivotal element of human culture and human history. The Christian faith, in particular, intimately links us to God—who is both our source and our intended destination—and to our fellow human beings.

items.title: Wednesday, September 2, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus declares his mission: “I must proclaim the good news of the Kingdom of God, because for this purpose I have been sent.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 3:1-9

And so, brothers and sisters, I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but rather as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for solid food. Even now you are still not ready, for you are still of the flesh. For as long as there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not of the flesh, and behaving according to human inclinations? For when one says, “I belong to Paul,” and another, “I belong to Apollos,” are you not merely human?

What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters have a common purpose, and each will receive wages according to the labor of each. For we are God’s servants, working together; you are God’s field, God’s building.

Psalm
Psalm 33:12-13, 14-15, 20-21

Happy is the nation whose God is the Lord,
    the people whom he has chosen as his heritage.
The Lord looks down from heaven;
    he sees all humankind.
From where he sits enthroned he watches
    all the inhabitants of the earth—
he who fashions the hearts of them all,
    and observes all their deeds.
Our soul waits for the Lord;
    he is our help and shield.
Our heart is glad in him,
    because we trust in his holy name.

Gospel Reading
Luke 4:38-44

After leaving the synagogue he entered Simon’s house. Now Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they asked him about her. Then he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. Immediately she got up and began to serve them.

As the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various kinds of diseases brought them to him; and he laid his hands on each of them and cured them. Demons also came out of many, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Messiah.

At daybreak he departed and went into a deserted place. And the crowds were looking for him; and when they reached him, they wanted to prevent him from leaving them. But he said to them, “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose.” So he continued proclaiming the message in the synagogues of Judea.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus declares his mission: “I must proclaim the good news of the Kingdom of God, because for this purpose I have been sent.” And he continues to pursue his mission among us in our efforts to do the work of evangelization.

Do we need evangelization? The statistics couldn’t be clearer. Did you know that the fastest-growing category in polls of religious affiliation is “none”? And did you know that there are far more nones than Catholics in this country?

So, Catholics cannot avoid the demand of evangelization, proclaiming the faith. Vatican II couldn’t be clearer on this score, seeing the Church itself as nothing but a vehicle for evangelization: It’s not so much the case that the Church has a mission, but rather that a mission has the Church.

St. Paul VI and St. John Paul II made this idea central to their teaching. In fact, John Paul famously called for a new evangelization. Bringing people to Christ is not one work among many; rather, it is the central work of the Church, that around which everything else that we do revolves.
